pages: You arrived after dark with a bag and Nell's address. The key was under the third flowerpot, just as she'd said.
You remember carrying your things upstairs. After that, mostly the bed. Now there's daylight across the floor and someone moving about below.
A corner of paper peeks out from under the mug on the desk.

lines: There's bread in the tin. I'll be back around lunchtime.
The little one on the shelf is Hotaru. I've been out on calls all week, so she's mostly been asleep.
The terminal on the desk is linked to Hotaru. Send her a hello if you need a hand.

stairs.dormant: The stairs lead down to Nell's workshop. Hotaru is still dozing on the shelf.
stairs.awake: The stairs lead down to Nell's workshop.
stairs.tablet: Nell’s slate is still on the bed.

after_greeting.title: Your first page is saved
after_greeting.hint: Hotaru is up. Nell's workshop is downstairs; the job board and repair benches are worth a look.

street_doors: Nell has left the street doors latched while she's out. The stairs lead back to your room.

workshop_after_greeting.title: The morning round is ready
workshop_after_greeting.hint: Your routines are saved. Nell is still out on calls; the workshop lights are yours to try.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: The workshop is warmer than the loft. A knot of shavings has collected beneath the vice; beside it, someone has set a stool out from the bench.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: Nell made room for you last night.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: She was down here after you’d gone to bed.

choices.reply: At the long bench. Keep the narrow drawer clear; she opens it with her knee.

choices.text: Is there anything I can do?
choices.reply: There’s a ticket on the board. She pinned it before she went out.
You were asleep before she’d found the spare key.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: Hotaru looks past you towards the stairs.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: Nell left a ticket for the stair light. It was my job to put it on.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: The ticket is soft along one edge. It has spent some time in a coat pocket.

pages.speaker: ticket
pages.text:
STAIR LIGHT
Relay replaced. Fitting checked.
Return to service before evening.
— N.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: The glass cracked on Tuesday. Nell put it right yesterday.

choices.reply: The new relay has a different address. The saved routine still calls the old one.

choices.text: It was dark when I arrived.
choices.reply: She meant to have it done before then.
Yes. The slate only listens at arm’s length, so we’ll have to stand beside it.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: In smaller writing: landing-lamp. Two more names follow it: repair-light, assembly-light.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: Leave the stair light on. She’ll be carrying things when she comes back.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: The lantern is on the wall at the foot of the stairs. Hold the slate up to it and ask.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: The lantern warms from the centre out. Light catches the underside of the handrail.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: There.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: For a moment she says nothing else. There is a pencilled card beside the vice.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: She left the tables off while she was changing it. We used to bring them on together.

choices.reply: The long bench and the assembly table. The card has all three addresses.

choices.text: Did you write the old card?
choices.reply: Nell wrote it. I used to read out the names while she checked them.
I’ll stay here.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: The rest of the card is a short list. The last name has a check beside it; the first two have none.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: The screen on the wall reaches all three at once. You’ll have to stand at it, though.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: Under the work lights, the rubbed edges of Nell’s tools show silver. The little labels on the drawers can be read from the bench.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: That’s the morning round.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: Nell will want that routine kept.

choices.reply: Top one. She’ll look there first.
The gate light. Nell’s ticket is behind this one.
She said lunchtime. There’s another cup by the stove.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: Behind the workshop card is a complaint from the north gate. Nell has crossed out ‘lamp replaced’ and written only: ‘Again?’

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: That one came back yesterday.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: Oh. Morning.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: You’re the one in the loft, then? I’m Hotaru.

choices.reply: I heard your bag on the stairs. I thought Nell was moving things again.

choices.text: Nell said you could show me around.
choices.reply: Of course. She’s left a few things here for you. Have you found the paper drawer?

choices.text: Have you been asleep all week?
choices.reply: Most of it. Nell’s been taking the calls herself. Is it still morning?

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: Nell left you the desk. The drawers stick a little; lift them as you pull.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: There’s a work ticket downstairs. Nell should be back for lunch.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: She came up again after you’d gone to sleep. The board by the bed always gives her away.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: She left something on the quilt. Twelve inches by eight, set down very square.

choices.reply: I couldn’t say from here. It’s mostly one flat edge.
Only ‘there’. She says that when a thing is sitting right.
It hasn’t moved all night. I’d have heard.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: Pick it up before you go down. She didn’t leave it there for the bed’s benefit.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: It is lighter than it looks, and warm from the window. A grey cord trails from one edge and ends in a brass plug no thicker than a pencil.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: That’s the field slate. She used to carry it everywhere.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: She’d hold it against whatever was misbehaving and ask what the matter was.

choices.reply: Mostly it said ‘fault’, in capitals. Nell found that helpful.
The screen downstairs. There’s a socket under the glass, with a brass collar.
Was. She put it where you’d trip over it. That’s how she hands things over.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: It’s on the wall by the long bench. The only thing along there that isn’t wood.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: The street doors swing out onto warm cobbles. Somewhere below the wall, a tram bell rings once and stops.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: Four days since I was last out here. Someone’s chalked squares on the cobbles since then.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: And Braum’s painted his fence again. That makes three coats this month.

choices.reply: Next door. He builds things. Mostly that fence.
Until the twenty-to-eight comes up. Then it’s quiet with a tram in it.
Down to the square. Sixty-three of them. I counted on the way down once, and on the way up to check.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: Nell comes back up that way with the bread. You hear the gate before you see her.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: Beyond the gate, the lane opens onto Spindle Walk. A little garden sits beside the steps down to the square.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: That’s the Rootwell in the middle. Nell stops there on the way back. Every time. I’ve counted.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: Under the glass a root glows the colour of strong tea. The needle on its dial sits low.

pages.speaker: braum
pages.text: You there. From Nell's, are you?

choices.reply: Thought so. Saw your bag go past last night.
Nothing I've built. The new sign. Well, the talking part of it.
Not wrong. Waiting. There's a difference, though Iona's stopped agreeing with me.

pages.speaker: braum
pages.text: Braum. Next door. I've put a frame up by the tram steps. Iona's doing the sign.

pages.speaker: braum
pages.text: She wanted Nell for the message card. You've got her slate. Would you have a look?

choices.reply: Good. Beside the tram steps. Mind the fresh edge on the step.

choices.text: What does it need to do?
choices.reply: Say where we are. Then a couple of useful things. It currently says where we are very firmly.

choices.text: Later. I have something to finish.
choices.reply: Right. I'll be up there. The frame won't wander.

pages.speaker: braum
pages.text: I'll let her know you're about. She's by the new glass board.

pages.speaker: iona
pages.text: Braum said you had Nell's slate. Did she send you?

choices.reply: Fair enough. Come round this side. You can see it better from here.

choices.text: I've only done the workshop lights.
choices.reply: Then we'll try it before leaving anything running.
That's the plug I was waiting for.

pages.speaker: iona
pages.text: Iona Venn. I painted the old board. This one's got a message card instead of a second coat.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: The glass reads WELCOME TO SPINDLE LANE. A moment later, it reads WELCOME TO SPINDLE LANE again.

pages.speaker: iona
pages.text: Braum says it is welcoming. He has a point.

pages.speaker: iona
pages.text: It's meant to change. Two or three messages. You can choose the last one.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: Where does the next one go?

pages.speaker: iona
pages.text: On the card, I hope. That's the part I asked Nell about.

pages.speaker: ticket
pages.text:
TRAM LANDING
Two or three messages.
Keep the lettering readable.
Payment: 25 p.
— Iona Venn

pages.speaker: iona
pages.text: The socket's below the glass. Bring the slate over and we'll see what you've written.

pages.speaker: iona
pages.text: There. I can read it before it changes.

pages.speaker: braum
pages.text: Even I know which stop it is now.

pages.speaker: iona
pages.text: You're standing under the nameplate.

pages.speaker: braum
pages.text: Helps.

pages.speaker: iona
pages.text: The last page is yours. What did you think?

choices.reply: I can read it from the steps. That's what I needed.

choices.text: I put my own words in.
choices.reply: Good. Anyone waiting here will have time to read them.

choices.text: It runs with the slate put away?
choices.reply: That's the idea. Come past tomorrow; I don't want to be here pressing anything.

pages.speaker: braum
pages.text: What was your name, then?

pages.speaker: player
pages.text: {player_name}.

pages.speaker: braum
pages.text: Right, {player_name}. I'll tell Nell. Can't keep calling you the one with the bag.

pages.speaker: iona
pages.text: Twenty-five pence. That's the message work settled. Haverlund Savings is down in the square, if you'd rather bank it.

nell-evening.title: The lamps that passed the test

pages.speaker: nell
pages.text: Good. You found the slate. I had a whole speech ready if you’d tried to repair the kettle with a fork.

pages.speaker: nell
pages.text: I saw the new sign from the tram. Iona paid you, I hope. She once tried to settle an invoice with a very fine drawing of the money.

pages.speaker: player
pages.text: Did the lamps go as well?

pages.speaker: nell
pages.text: They worked on my bench. Both of them. Out here they wait all day for the dark, then decide they’ve earned the night off. Look at their closing card.

pages.speaker: nell
pages.text: Read the card the way the lamp does. It’s dark: what does it ask for? Now it’s daylight. Ask again.

choices.text: So the bulbs are all right?
choices.reply: I checked them twice. Don’t let a clever fault talk you into buying a new bulb.

choices.text: Could I just leave them on?
choices.reply: You could. Then we’d be paying for daylight. Try your card in the sun as well as the dark.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: I can try it in daylight and in the dark while we stand here. No waiting until breakfast.

pages.speaker: nell
pages.text: Two lamps, same rule. Finish that and we’ll call it a day. Eighteen pence. I’m paying for the checking too.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: The two lamps stay dark in the last of the daylight. Then the clock turns over, and they come on together, as if they’d agreed it between them.

pages.speaker: nell
pages.text: There.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: And the same clock, wherever we go.

pages.speaker: nell
pages.text: The hall’s Public Works desk has more of this sort of thing. Mira will find you. She finds everyone.

pages.speaker: nell
pages.text: Tonight, put the slate down before your tea goes cold.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: A woman in a plum field jacket is standing at the service screen with a folder pressed flat against the glass, writing on it with the pencil she isn’t holding in her teeth.

pages.speaker: mira
pages.text: You’re Nell’s lodger. The one with the slate.

choices.reply: Good. Nell said to look for the cord. I’ve been looking at people’s collars all morning.
Mira. Public Works. Maps, mostly, and whatever the maps say is wrong.
The cord. Nobody else in town walks about with a plug.

pages.speaker: mira
pages.text: The hall gave me five jobs and one pair of hands. Mine. They’re all in the square, and none of them need a ladder.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: Which of them need a slate?

pages.speaker: mira
pages.text: All of them. Since the conduits went in, the benches and stalls here take instructions. Where to face. Where to stand. The screen passes your routine along if you’re standing at it.

pages.speaker: mira
pages.text: Start with the band. Saturday, round the Rootwell. Half the benches are looking at the harbour.

choices.reply: Nothing. It isn’t playing on Saturday.
Seven. I counted twice. The first time I’d counted one I was sitting on.
Iron frames. Also, I’d like it done once properly, so it can be done again.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: She tears the top ticket off the folder and holds it out without looking up. Her other hand is already marking something on a map of the square.

pages.speaker: mira
pages.text: The Rootwell is at y twenty-four. My map says so, and for once the square agrees.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: Seven benches turn their backs on the sea. A pigeon on the end of one disapproves, and leaves.

pages.speaker: mira
pages.text: Good. They can see the Rootwell now. Whether they want to is the band’s problem.

pages.speaker: mira
pages.text: Next one’s on Spindle Walk. There’s a gap in the middle where a bench used to be, before somebody borrowed it for the physic garden.

choices.text: How far apart should they be?
choices.reply: Six metres. I walked it. It’s the distance where two people on two benches don’t have to listen to each other.
Nobody admits it. The garden is very pleased with it.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: Six metres is a long way for me. I’ll count it from the railing.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: Mira unfolds the square map against the screen and writes something small across the arrival lawn, in pencil.

pages.speaker: mira
pages.text: Lodger’s corner. Pencil, because the hall will want a meeting before it’s ink.

pages.speaker: mira
pages.text: That’s all five. In order, too. The hall will find that suspicious.

choices.reply: Not from me. But Tessa’s been at my elbow all week about The Pantry’s board, and Ada Kettering left a note at the hall entirely in capitals.
It goes in the drawer with the others. Then somebody moves a bench and I start a new one.
Thank the band. They’re the ones who’ll have somewhere to look.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: She folds the map, then stops, and looks past you at the dial on the Rootwell.

pages.speaker: mira
pages.text: Four, last month. Three and a half now. I write it down every Thursday.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: Is it meant to go down?

pages.speaker: mira
pages.text: I don’t know. That’s why I write it down.

pages.speaker: mira
pages.text: The shops by the market have jobs for your slate. They pay better than I do. Everyone does.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: The bell over the door hasn’t finished before a voice comes from behind the oven.

pages.speaker: ada
pages.text: If it’s the second batch, it’s at eleven. If it’s the first, you’re too late. If it’s me, I’m busy.

choices.text: Mira sent me about the board.
choices.reply: Did she. Then you’re the slate.
The one with the slate. Nell said you’d be round eventually.
Everything smells good at seven. Come back at four and tell me that.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: She comes round the oven, wiping her hands on a cloth that has been floury for longer than you’ve been alive.

pages.speaker: ada
pages.text: Ada Kettering. Morning Loaf. Forty-one years, same oven, same back door.

pages.speaker: ada
pages.text: And every morning somebody knocks on that back door to ask when the next batch is. Seven, nine and eleven. Every two hours. It isn’t a secret. I just don’t want to say it forty times.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: You’ve said it twice since we came in.

pages.speaker: ada
pages.text: Then put it on the board. All three. The board’s by the window, and it takes the slate.

choices.text: Why not write it in chalk?
choices.reply: I did. Somebody rubbed it out to write MIND THE STEP. There is no step.
There is no afternoon. There’s me, sitting down.
Good. Don’t touch the oven. It doesn’t know you.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: BATCH AT 7. BATCH AT 9. BATCH AT 11. The board works through them while Ada watches with her arms folded.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: Nobody has knocked since the board came on.

pages.speaker: ada
pages.text: It’s been four minutes.

pages.speaker: ada
pages.text: Still. That’s a record.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: She puts a paper bag on the counter. It’s warm, and folded over twice so you can’t see in.

pages.speaker: ada
pages.text: For Nell. She’ll say she doesn’t want it. Fifteen pence for you; it’s in the corner of the bag, so don’t eat that bit.

pages.speaker: tessa
pages.text: Oh good, it’s you. Mira said you’d come by, and I said you wouldn’t have time, and she bet me a lemon.

pages.speaker: tessa
pages.text: I owe her a lemon.

choices.reply: My cousin Teo’s. I bring the orchard down on market days and mind the counter while he’s up at the farms buying everything else. He leaves before it’s light.
Teo. My cousin. He signs his name like a man settling a debt.
The board. Come and look at it.

pages.speaker: tessa
pages.text: Teo writes the prices on that slate every morning, then changes them twice, then I rub out the board and copy them, and by the time I’ve finished he’s changed one again.

pages.speaker: tessa
pages.text: Apples are four. Lemons are three. Plums were six until the Kerrigans’ cart came up full, so now they’re five. That’s the one that always gets missed.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: The board only says APPLES 4P.

pages.speaker: tessa
pages.text: It’s said that since Tuesday. People think we’ve stopped selling everything else.

choices.text: Can the slate hold a price list?
choices.reply: Teo says yes. Teo also says the cart will be here by six.
The Kerrigans grow too many, then feel guilty about it. Five, anyway.
Thank you. I’ll weigh you an apple. On the house. Well, on Teo.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: APPLES 4P. LEMONS 3P. PLUMS 5P. A woman comes in, reads the board twice, and buys a bag of plums without asking a single question.

pages.speaker: tessa
pages.text: Did you see that? Nobody buys plums without asking.

pages.speaker: tessa
pages.text: Teo will want to change everything tomorrow. Leave him the list where he can find it. One number each, that’s all he has to touch.

pages.speaker: tessa
pages.text: Eighteen pence. And the apple. Don’t argue about the apple.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: A woman at the cutting table looks up, takes three pins out of her mouth and puts them in a cushion before she says anything.

pages.speaker: gret
pages.text: You’ll be the one with Nell’s slate. Your left shoulder sits lower than your right. That’s the satchel.

choices.reply: It’s common. I only mention it so you know I’m looking.
Mira sends everyone. Half my orders are pockets for that jacket of hers.
Finch. Thread was my father’s joke. He thought it sounded like a firm of solicitors.

pages.speaker: gret
pages.text: Gret Finch. I make coats, I take them in, I let them out. Mostly out, after the winter.

pages.speaker: gret
pages.text: Fourteen orders finished on that rail. Two collected. The rest of the town thinks I’m slow.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: The tag on the navy coat says NOT BY LUNCH.

pages.speaker: gret
pages.text: That one’s Braum’s. He tells everybody his things will be done by lunch. It seemed only fair.

pages.speaker: gret
pages.text: I don’t chase people. I’d like the board to do it for me. The name, then READY, in capitals, so they notice. Braum, Iona and Mira first; theirs have waited longest.

choices.reply: Braum reads the board from the tram, and the tram doesn’t stop for long.
I’ve measured all three of them. That’s quite personal enough for one year.
Thank you. Write the ticket once and use it three times. I’d do the same with a pattern.

pages.speaker: narration
pages.text: BRAUM READY. IONA READY. MIRA READY. Within the hour, the bell over the door goes twice.

pages.speaker: gret
pages.text: Iona came for her apron. She read the board from across the square and said the letters were well spaced. From her, that’s a medal.

pages.speaker: hotaru
pages.text: Braum hasn’t come.

pages.speaker: gret
pages.text: He will. He’ll say he was on his way anyway.

pages.speaker: gret
pages.text: Twenty pence. And when that satchel strap goes, bring it here before you tie a knot in it.

haverlund-lane: Mind the chalk squares. Somebody’s halfway through a game.
That’s Pepper on the wall. The notice says she doesn’t come when called. The notice is right.
The lamp by the gate has a wire all the way from the square. Nobody’s told it what to do yet.
The twenty-to-eight was late again. I could hear the bell from the shelf.
waiting-ticket: Nell pinned the ticket by the window.
The little drawer under the vice sticks. Mind your fingers.
landing-light: I’ll keep out of the way while you try it.
Nell left the fitting checked. The address is on her ticket.
morning-round: The two work lights belong on that card as well.
She usually starts at the long bench.
finished: There’s still warmth in the kettle.
haverlund-square: The clock’s been five minutes fast since spring. Nell still sets her watch by it.
That little one takes the parcels round. It waits for the handles to stop swinging before it goes.
You can smell the first batch from the top of the steps. Getting back up is harder.
shop-bakery: It’s warmer by the oven than at the stove at home. Don’t tell Nell.
The tins on the bottom shelf are the oldest. Ada sells them first.
shop-greengrocer: Every crate has two tags. One of them is Tessa’s handwriting.
The scale has an apple in it. I think it lives there.
shop-tailor: One row of thread is out of order. Two blues have swapped.
The mirror makes the room twice as long. I checked the other side.
band-seats: Seven benches. Some of them look at the sea on purpose, I think.
Mira’s map says the Rootwell is at twenty-four. So does the Rootwell.
next-batch: Seven, nine, eleven. Two apart each time.
Ada didn’t say anything about the oven. I don’t think it’s on the ticket.

haverlund-lane.title: A welcome of your own
haverlund-lane.hint: Your messages are running at the tram landing. You can rewrite the card whenever you like. Press I to check your pay, or visit Haverlund Savings in the square.

haverlund-square.title: Rootward Square
haverlund-square.hint: The square is open to explore. Nell’s work tickets are still on the board back at the workshop.

city-hall.title: The public lobby
city-hall.hint: Enquiries can help you find your way. The Public Works desk keeps the current job book; the civic screen connects the hall’s lamps.

shop-bakery.title: Morning Loaf
shop-bakery.hint: Ada’s board is by the north window. Read her note on the frame, then jack the slate in below it.

shop-greengrocer.title: The Pantry
shop-greengrocer.hint: The price board is on the back wall. Teo’s note is underneath it.

shop-tailor.title: Finch & Thread
shop-tailor.hint: Gret’s order board is on the back wall, with the order book on its ledge.

tablet_waiting.title: Something on the quilt
tablet_waiting.hint: Nell left it on your bed. Hotaru thinks it is meant for you.
